commenti.body: It’s been quite awhile since I saw it, but the dominant theme that I remember was an exploration of free will.  Would we be better off to allow freedom of action if it means people will suffer harm or should we rigidly impose proper behavior?

yes, precisely. I struggle to *fully* understand why it concludes the way it does but generally, it says that free will has to come from the desire from deep within to change like what the priest says. You can't force someone to change their behaviours mechanically (enhance the title) because that's not truly changing them. It almost seems like a christian message if not for the way (I think?) the movie suggests how Alex will probably never change deep within and instead only direct his delinquent behaviour in a powerful systemic approach, much like his droogies. This is evident in how despite his thorough reading of the bible, he hilariously takes the wrong perspective on its morality tales. Is this Christian attitude that the priest puts forward futile for someone like Alex?

It's a more complex essay about violence in modern society, precisely a dystopian analysis. At first it shows how violence in young people  comes from poor education in family and society and from drugs. In the end it shows that violence comes from our inner nature and cannot be removed; it rules social relationships, victims turn into executioners and viceversa, depending on opportunities. Social government is based on the use of institutionalized violence (see police forces, armies and wars); not by chance droogs and Alex are recruited by government. At the same time it shows the strong influence of mass media; the Ludovico treatment is a form of istitutionalized violence. Removing violence is violence!

I take it to be an allegory on how morality is dictated by the strongest influence, similar to survival of the fittest but applied sociologically. For instance, Alex is shown to be the "top dog" of the droogs but is eventually consumed by a competing and larger pyramid (hierarchy) wherein he is forced to bend the knee. Similar to the *ape scenes, Alex became the submissive one in the equation and he was basically forced to conform. So the message is like: morality is just serving the interests of those more powerful than you, which is typical Kubrick nihilism.

The film takes these themes from the novel, and what it boils down to is Burgess's interest in the idea of free will but also as it links to original sin. 

Burgess was interested in a couple of things in his catholicism - Pelagianism vs Augustinianism: St Augustine believes we are all fallen due to original sin, that is our nature and it can't be programmed out, Pelagius says no - we are spotless souls and should strive to remain uncorrupted by the world. Burgess was also interested in Manichaeism - the deep struggle between good/evil, light/darkness. 

Essentially the core view that the novel (and film) poses is that it is better to be evil in our own free will and choose it, with the possibility of later developing organically (the organ "human" in Malay, or the sweet orange) and choosing good, than it is to be "good" or rule abiding as a sterile automaton (the clockwork). 

If you're further interested in this then Burgess was also interested in Skinner and his behavior modification of animals in order to have them be "good", too. 

Hope this helps.
This is a really interesting point, thanks for sharing.
thank you so much that is really interesting.

Keep in mind, the book had a final chapter that Kubrick left out. As with all Kubrick adaptations, it's your choice how much the book explains the film.

After all is said and done, Alex really does eventually become reformed. He finds a new group of droogs but is less and less satisfied with the ultra-violence. He ends up running into one of the original droogs, can't remember who, and finds him to be a regular grown man with a wife and job. Alex realizes he's much too grown to keep engaging in this behavior and decides to grow up. 

Again, Kubrick films and themes from the books don't always match. The book was far less dystopian than the film, with the ultra violence beginning a commentary on youth culture instead of culture in general.

It's about rehabilitation and the prison system being absolutely flawed. "When a man cannot choose, he ceases to be a man." Is it right to force Alex into being something he was clearly not? It's the predicament we must play in our heads about nature and chaos, and yes- totalitarianism. The priest in the prison explains the movies motives repeatedly.

When I first watched the movie, my initial thought was about how, for example former prisioners, will always carry a permanent stigma around them, regardless of how much they change. Alex becomes a perfectly kind person after the treatment, but people still treat him as the scum he once was.

I understand this isn't the universally accepted interpretation of the movie. Even I now think that the theme of "free will" fits much better with the movie, but what can I say? It's still the first thing I thought of, and I still think Kubrick wanted to make a brief mention to that in his film.

I think we should bring Stanley Kubrick's own words into this conversation. From a contemporary interview, answering a question about why the character of Alex fascinates audiences:

>I think that it’s probably because we can identify with Alex on the unconscious level. The psychiatrists tell us the unconscious has no conscience — and perhaps in our unconscious we are all potential Alexes. It may be that only as a result of morality, the law and sometimes our own innate character that we do not become like him. Perhaps this makes some people feel uncomfortable and partly explains some of the controversy which has arisen over the film. Perhaps they are unable to accept this view of human nature. But I think you find much the same psychological phenomena at work in Shakespeare’s *Richard III.* You should feel nothing but dislike towards Richard, and yet when the role is well played, with a bit of humour and charm, you find yourself gradually making a similar kind of identification with him.

Malcolm McDowell has also compared the character to Richard III in [interviews;](https://www.theguardian.com/film/2019/apr/02/how-we-made-a-clockwork-orange-malcolm-mcdowell-stanley-kubrick) both characters are superficial charmers ultimately about appeasing their own base desires. As Kubrick notes, that is a disturbing aspect of both works -- the possibility that our fascination and even identification with these characters says something about our own dark desires.

>It's a film that demonstrates the terrible things people can do if they don't reflect on their moral choices and instead allow their choices to be dictated to them by a higher power. It's a way for them to avoid responsibility of their moral choices and it explains the cruelty humans can inherit once in a big enough group.

This is, of course, precisely the logic of totalitarianism: the desire to avoid all of the messy, complicated, morally ambiguous realities of life, to start again from year zero within a system that explains and controls everything. A hope for a world where individuals don't have to make difficult moral choices because they live inside an all-encompassing ideology.

A relevant CS Lewis quote:

> If a thing is free to be good it's also free to be bad. And free will is what has made evil possible. Why, then, did God give them free will? Because free will, though it makes evil possible, is also the only thing that makes possible any love or goodness or joy worth having. A world of automata -of creatures that worked like machines- would hardly be worth creating.
